summary: A document cannot be read as it stood, or as it will stand, on a date: eta has no valid_from, valid_to
detail: Carried forward from Genoa (2013, ~/Workshop/archive/post-peleton/Genoa/src/genoa/core/valid_from_valid_to.py), where hedge-fund use needed 'what did we believe on the 3rd'. Genoa's shape: an update closes the current row (valid_to = now) and inserts a new one under the same `ref`; `valid_on(date)` filters any query; many-to-many relations carry their own valid range; `find_or_create` on a date respects a version already dated in the future. Two kinds of time are involved, and eta has only one. Transaction time (when a write was recorded) is the ledger's -- delta's `delta_ledger`: ops, inverse and `at` per entry, so a document registered with the ledger can already be walked back to any moment, but only while the recorded paths still mean what they meant before the schema changed. Valid time (when something is true in the world: a price effective from Monday, a deal term that changes next quarter) is what Genoa's valid_from/valid_to gave and the ledger cannot, because it is written now about later. Design questions: (a) derive as-at reads from the ledger, with no schema change, or (b) put valid_from/valid_to on the tables and give a document's read() an `at`, or both, one for each kind of time; (c) name it as delta did, with the date in the document's name (`venue-at:42:2026-06-16`), so an as-at document is read-only and seen like any other; (d) how undo treats a future-dated write. Start with a story, per CLAUDE.md, not a feature: stories.md's Open 'Time' (the wedding's deadline, a story with a `when`) is where it meets the harness.

summary: No page is drawn from a document's shape: every view is placed by hand, and nothing lets a named component override a type's drawing
detail: The second thing carried forward from Genoa/Landfall (~/Workshop/archive/post-peleton/overview.md), and the thread the line has kept picking up. Landfall (2013): Genoa's describe_model() published every model's properties and types; `{label, model}` in ui.js gave a working list/view/edit panel; each value's template was looked up by `<mode>-<type>` (viewcell, editcell, inlinecell, viewfield, editfield), last registered wins, so one override changed every Image column; the settings, then a custom `js` panel, went further. It is what let Betts and Gilbert build fund screens without the architect, and most of Gilbert's 102 commits went into those generic screens. Since then: zeta DEC-10 (13 Sep 2026) derived a screen from a TypeScript `Table` that a test checks against the live schema (`zeta/describe.ts` is Genoa's describe.py again), with few rules in `zeta/derive.ts` and anything beyond them a hand-written node; apples' panel: every row has one, derived from the declaration, the same panel from every reading; hjeli's derive-ux in an earlier app. eta has the pieces but no derivation: bento's boxPage/collectionPage, `choice`, `row`, `cell`; applets registered by name (`registerApplet`, last wins, the same mechanism as data-micro) but placed by hand in each view (the wedding's picture-field is Landfall's editfield-image again). The tension is with eta's own rules: 'Build nothing no story needs', 'Not generated code', and the 17 Sep review's YAGNI D. So derive at render time, never generate files; derive from the document (what read() returns, or a declaration the database vouches for, as zeta did), never from the entity; let a type name an applet, so an override is a registration, not an edit to every view. Questions: (a) what a document declares about itself (types, labels, which paths are writable, which the permit already says); (b) whether the permit table and the page come from the same declaration; (c) where the override ladder stops, and write it down: Landfall's most powerful hooks (type templates, swapping controls, page blocks) were never documented; (d) the evidence: which screens did Landfall's users actually live in, custom or generic? Start with a story no example tells yet: reference data nobody would write a story for, e.g. 'The couple add a venue, and it is in the list' with no view written for venues.
note: 2026-09-24: added after comparing eta with Genoa/Landfall. Open, for Peter.

summary: Paging and streaming: no story yet reads past the first page or receives a result over time
detail: Landfall (2013) had it from the start: genoa_list(model, criteria, offset, limit, summary, order_by) answered {items, count, summary}; table_limit 24 on a desktop, 10 on a phone, -1 for all; a pagination template; per-collection limits; totals (sum, avg) worked out over the whole filtered set, not the page. eta today: chat holds a room whole in memory, as one delta document, and shows its last 50 messages (documents/room.ts), so more is held than before and nothing reaches older ones; bento's find dims and counts, never hides, so a filter doesn't reduce what is sent; every write redraws each reader's whole page on the server and diffs it against the page last sent, which server.ts keeps per connection, so cost grows with page size times readers. concept found whole-document transport breaks at ~5k records, and concept/scale.md has real sizes (85k allocations, 40k areas). Two things, related: PAGING, a window onto a collection, and STREAMING, rows arriving over time (a feed, a long result from a Bun `$` callout or an outside queue written back as facts, a slow first page). Much of the machinery exists: doc names are data, and compartment.ts already expects 'one whose name is criteria (this month's appointments, last month's)'; the address (`path?what=which`) could carry the window, so the back button pages; parts.ts already sends rows added to or removed from a list as `after`/`before`/`remove`, which is the wire shape of streaming. Questions: (a) the window in the document's name (`room:general?before=812`) or in the tray's address; (b) who is told: a write lands on `room:general`, and reading() records the name the page read, so a window's readers are told only if the window reads its base document too, or the kernel learns that one name belongs to a family of names; (c) keyset (before=id) or offset: an offset moves under a concurrent insert (room.ts line 31 uses LIMIT 1 OFFSET), a keyset does not; (d) totals and counts over the whole set are a read of their own, as the wedding's counts already are; (e) the harness: a cast whose pages are windows, and `seen`/`unseen` for someone who has scrolled away. Stories to start from: 'Ada scrolls back past the first fifty messages and reads what Bob said yesterday'; 'Bob speaks while Ada is reading old messages, and her place does not move'.
note: 2026-09-24: added after comparing eta with Genoa/Landfall. Distributed work itself is out of scope (Bun `$` or a queue, not eta or delta); only how its result arrives belongs here. Open, for Peter.

summary: Stale writes: two people changing one value, and the last write silently wins
detail: Genoa (2013) had optimistic locking: a `Versioned` model carried `_version_`, a save sent the version it was based on, and `from_pairs` raised 'Version mismatch' on a stale one (Genoa/src/genoa/access/versioned.py). An eta write carries no base version, and PatchOp is add, replace and remove only, so two people replacing one path both land, in arrival order, and the first never learns it was overwritten. `data-write-on="input"` (debounced, K3) makes it likelier: a field is written while someone else reads it. RFC 6902 already has the guard: a `test` op, which fails the whole patch unless the value at the path is what the writer saw; eta's three verbs stay three, and `test` is a condition, not a change. Alternatives: the version the page was drawn at, sent with the write and checked against the document's version (coarser: any write to the document refuses, not just one to the same path). Questions: (a) `test` per path or version per document; (b) what the refused writer sees (see n5); (c) whether undo and redo, which apply a recorded inverse, carry a test of their own, since walking back over someone else's later write is the same problem; (d) the harness needs two members writing one path. Story: 'Ann and Bob both change the notional; Bob's is refused, and he sees Ann's.'
note: 2026-09-24: from the Genoa/Landfall comparison. Open, for Peter.

summary: Whose history: the ledger records per document, so a row written through two documents has its history split
detail: Genoa (2013) audited per row: Audit held the entity's type and primary key, before-values, what changed and who, for every create, update, delete and many-to-many add or remove, whichever screen made the change, and get_audit_trail(obj) answered 'what happened to this deal'. eta's ledger is keyed by document (`<docType>:<docId>`), with ops as JSON Pointer paths into that document. When one row can be written through two documents, its history is split: in the wedding, a claim (`wedding_claims`) is made through a household and removed through the couple's board when its gift is deleted, and guests and ask replies are written through both, so one row's history is under `board:…` and `household:…`, at different paths. An auditor, or 'why is the casserole the Okafors'?', asks about the thing, not the screen. Options: (a) a rule: every row has exactly one owning document, and other documents only read it (documents-history.md's open question 5, 'every field has exactly one writing actor', said again for rows), which the harness or a test could check; (b) a ledger index by entity: patch() reports the rows it touched alongside the ops, so history can be asked by row; (c) accept it and let history be asked across documents by a join the example writes. It also affects n1: reading a row as it stood on a date needs to know where its history is. Story: 'The couple ask who claimed the casserole and when, and see the Okafors' claim and Ben's withdrawn one.'
note: 2026-09-24: from the Genoa/Landfall comparison. Related to n1. Open, for Peter. 2026-09-25 review: lowered to low: no story asks for it yet.

summary: Identity is pluggable for passwords, not yet for a provider that must refuse the socket (SSO, OAuth2, LDAP, the CLI)
detail: Authorization is already pluggable (permit, own, resolveDoc and reading(), Example.active); authentication is not. server.ts's `/ws` takes the `session_id` cookie or makes a random UUID and upgrades; ConnectionData is `{ sessionId }`; an example cannot refuse an upgrade or attach a verified identity, and cannot replace /ws ('a kernel route of the same path wins'). Every connection is an anonymous visit, and logging in is a write to the session document that the example's compartment judges: the wedding checks an invitation code (`replace /code`, kindOf) against its tables; chat's `/name` is no authentication at all. That is the database as the identity provider, done per example. It is fine for a shared code and wrong for a password: a password sent as a patch sits in the client's `window.eta.inspect().lastSent` and op log and may be echoed to the session's tabs. Genoa (2013) had the same split: AccessControl._login_ against the Person table, then Robert Betts's LDAPMixin overriding _login_ with an LDAP bind (Genoa/src/genoa/access/ldap_mixin.py): one method, swapped. The shape for eta: a provider is (1) HTTP routes on Example.routes (db or LDAP: POST /login with credentials; OAuth2: GET /login redirecting with state and PKCE, GET /callback exchanging the code with fetch and verifying the id_token), and (2) what they all end with: a verified identity and roles, a FRESH session_id cookie (never the pre-login one: session fixation), and the session document written server-side through the example's own document patch() and notify(), with its identity and role paths refused over the wire by permit(). The kernel's one new seam: an optional `Example.identify(req)` called at /ws before the upgrade, returning the session id to use or a Response to refuse, so an example can require a login, accept a reverse proxy's header (SSO), or take a bearer token from the CLI (which keeps `.eta-session` today and would need to log in too). Per provider: db passwords with Bun.password (argon2/bcrypt, built in; Genoa used salted SHA-1); OAuth2 needs no dependency beyond fetch and crypto.subtle for JWKS (or `jose`, to ask about); LDAP needs a client (`ldapts`, to ask about, and a spike under Bun). Questions: (a) identity only in the session document (eta's way), or also on ConnectionData; (b) logout: clear the cookie, delete the visit, close the sockets; (c) one provider per example, or several (codes for guests, OAuth2 for the couple); (d) the harness: casts log in through the provider, or seed sessions with roles and test the provider on its own (a test directory in Docker, a fake OAuth2 issuer). Stories: 'A visitor without a login sees only the login page and cannot write'; 'Ann logs in and sees her desk'; 'Ann cannot give herself the admin role'.
note: 2026-09-24: from the Genoa/Landfall comparison and Peter: 'right now we use the db but we could use oauth2 or ldap'. Open, for Peter. 2026-09-25: leave signs people in with passwords: a sign-in route on Example.routes, a fresh session with sessionCookie(), who you are in the session document, refused over the wire; /ws checks Origin (n36 closed). Still open: the `identify(req)` seam before the upgrade (a reverse proxy's header, a bearer token from the CLI), OAuth2 and LDAP behind the same route shape, rate-limiting sign-in attempts, and sign-up.

summary: eta keeps its own JSON Pointer parse (it can go now) and applyPatch (it waits on delta #4) beside delta core's
detail: The pointer half can go now: delta 0.7.0's splitPath is strict RFC 6901 (it throws on a slashless path or a stray ~, and '/' is no longer the root), at least as strict as eta's parsePointer, and joinPath / escapeSegment build paths from ids. The swap is mechanical, across src/json-pointer.ts and about 12 example files. The applyPatch half waits on delta #4: delta core's applyOps sets a missing member on replace, ignores a missing remove and overwrites on add at an index, while eta's applyPatch throws on the first two and inserts on the third, and the harness relies on that throw (an applet sent ops that do not describe its props). Swap PatchOp for DeltaOp with it. The shared test vectors that would pin the two together are delta #15 (was eta #22).
note: 2026-09-24: waits on delta core. 2026-09-25 review: the pointer half is unblocked by delta 0.7.0; eta #22 (a wire law and shared vectors) is merged here and into delta #15.

summary: One document named by a live session's id stops the telling of its change to everyone
detail: tellChanges echoes to each socket with wireName, which throws, loudly and on purpose, for a document keyed by a live session id that is not `own`; the throw ends that change's echo and redraws for every socket after it (caught per listener in documents.ts). A per-socket guard would keep the others told while the failure is still reported.

summary: No shared blueshed plugin or router skill tells an agent which of eta, delta and railroad to use, and delta-doc's own description captures every 'live multi-user app' request before railroad or eta are considered
detail: architect.md §5: delta-doc's SKILL.md claims every 'live multi-user app' request (its description names greenfield apps choosing between Firebase, Supabase and the rest, and the body says 'the answer is delta-doc') and never mentions eta or railroad by name as an alternative; eta-app only fires inside the eta repo, so a greenfield 'build me a live app' request never reaches it even though eta's own README pitches exactly that. Proposed shape (architect §6.2, proposal-final §5): one `blueshed` plugin in a marketplace repo holding a router skill under about 800 words (the decision guide: different people see different slices of the same data, undo matters, forms and lists, one box -> eta; interaction-heavy UI, several processes, Postgres/RLS, other clients consuming the doc JSON -> delta + railroad; one very interactive widget inside eta -> an applet, optionally a railroad island; reactive UI with no sync -> railroad alone), plus WIRE.md, one sandbox hook, one release command and MCP wiring; package skills stay inside the npm packages, synced at session start, restricted to @blueshed/* plus an allowlist (delta's install-skills does this since 02b1926), and delta-doc's own description narrows to projects that have already chosen delta. Namespacing under `blueshed:` ends skill/command shadowing in multi-repo sessions (architect F2, now largely moot since delta re-syncs its vendored railroad skills at each railroad release) and retires each repo's own /publish once `release` lands. Same item in railroad's, delta's and eta's todo.jsonl. The plugin is also the home for shared test tooling (was railroad #14): the two-tab / waitFor browser-test helper is hand-copied in bun-route's reference.md, railroad's tests/webview.test.ts and a dogfooder's tests; eta's src/webview.ts (`at`, `waitFor`) is the tidied version. summary: The bento's rules say nothing about focus or the keyboard
detail: The kernel puts the page behind a modal `inert` (bento.ts, rule 14), but the eighteen rules never say where focus goes when a drawer or modal opens, what Escape does, or where focus returns when it closes. duckdown's editor had to decide each (its CLAUDE.md, 'Accessible by default'): a drawer is not modal, so it takes focus as it opens, Escape closes it, and focus goes back to what opened it; a modal is named by its heading and gives focus back when it is dropped, not only when closed; a chosen figure says so with aria-pressed/aria-current, never by a ring alone. summary: An applet's ctx.send answers nothing, so an applet cannot learn its own write was refused
detail: window.eta.send(doc, ops) resolves with the write's answer by its id -- echoed, refused with its reason, unanswered, unsent (n88) -- but AppletContext.send is `(doc, ops) => void`. An applet that sends a gesture's write (a drag let go) cannot hear that the planner refused it, nor why. Reproduced in japan-eta: carrying Willem's face, the only one on the Yanaka walk, onto teamLab is refused ("Willem is the only one on Yanaka old-town walk: moving Willem would put all eight of you on it."); with ctx.send the gestures overlay's stand-in faded after four seconds and nothing was said. japan-eta works around it by calling window.eta!.send from the applet (src/applets/gestures-applet.ts, the let-go; its todo n15). The cost of the workaround: the applet reaches past its context to a global, and a test that mounts the applet with a stand-in context cannot see the answer. Want: ctx.send returns the same Promise<Answer> as window.eta.send.

summary: A story compares a page with a watched document as it is written out, so a row an undo puts back, now last in delta's copy, fails "undo did not restore"
